passages.happening:
Hezekiah becomes king at twenty-five and reigns twenty-nine years, ‘And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father David had done’ (verse 2). ‘In the first month of the first year of his reign, Hezekiah opened and repaired the doors of the house of the LORD’ (verse 3).

He gathers the priests and Levites and tells them to consecrate themselves and the house of the LORD, and to remove every impurity from the Holy Place (verse 5). ‘For our fathers were unfaithful and did evil in the sight of the LORD our God’ (verse 6); they shut the doors and put out the lamps, and wrath came on Judah (verses 7-9). ‘Now it is in my heart to make a covenant with the LORD, the God of Israel, so that His fierce anger will turn away from us’ (verse 10). Levites from every clan consecrate themselves and cleanse the house, carrying every unclean thing out to the Kidron Valley; in sixteen days the work is done (verses 12-19).
passages.hearers:
The previous chapter ended with Ahaz shutting the doors of the house of the LORD; this one opens with his son throwing them open. Chronicles gives Hezekiah more space than any king after Solomon, and it begins not with his wars or his building but with worship. Chapter 29 restores the temple, chapter 30 the Passover, chapter 31 the offerings, and only then, in chapter 32, does Assyria arrive. For the Chronicler, Hezekiah is almost a second Solomon.

His dates are one of the harder problems in biblical chronology. Many date his reign about 715 to 686 BC; others place his accession around 727 or 726 BC. Either way he ruled in the shadow of Assyria, which destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 BC. Kings sums up his reform in a few verses and gives most of its space to Sennacherib; Chronicles reverses the proportions. The first month of his first year may mean his first full year, and it places the cleansing just before the time of Passover.

God's presence required that his house be kept holy. Unclean things, the idol objects of Ahaz's reign, had to be removed, and they were carried to the Kidron Valley, where Asa had burned Maacah's image. Only priests could enter the inner building, so they carried things out to the court, and the Levites took them from there. Hezekiah's speech follows a pattern the Chronicler uses often: confession of the fathers' sins, the consequences, a resolve to make a covenant, berit, and a call to act. The list of Levites names men from every clan and from the three guilds of singers: the whole tribe took part.
passages.later: Kings sums up his reign: ‘Hezekiah trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel. No king of Judah was like him, either before him or after him’ (2 Kings 18:5).
passages.asks: Hezekiah's first act was to open what his father had shut. Ask what door to God has been shut in your life or your household, and whether you could open it this month. And ask what needs carrying out before worship can begin again.

passages.happening:
Early in the morning Hezekiah gathers the officials and goes up to the house of the LORD. Bulls, rams, lambs and goats are offered as a sin offering for the kingdom, the sanctuary and Judah; the king and the assembly lay their hands on the goats, and the priests make atonement for all Israel (verses 20-24). He stations the Levites with cymbals, harps and lyres as David, Gad and Nathan had commanded (verse 25). ‘When the burnt offering began, the song of the LORD and the trumpets began as well, accompanied by the instruments of David king of Israel’ (verse 27), and the whole assembly worships until it is finished (verse 28).

The Levites sing praises ‘in the words of David and of Asaph the seer’ (verse 30). The people bring sacrifices and thank offerings, and ‘all whose hearts were willing’ bring burnt offerings (verse 31). There are too few priests, and the Levites help them, ‘For the Levites had been more diligent in consecrating themselves than the priests had been’ (verse 34). ‘Then Hezekiah and all the people rejoiced at what God had prepared for the people, because everything had been accomplished so quickly’ (verse 36).
passages.hearers:
The sacrifices follow the patterns of Leviticus. A sin offering, sometimes called a purification offering, dealt with the defilement of sin; laying hands on the goats identified the worshipers with the offering. Atonement, kipper, is the removal of sin's guilt and defilement so that fellowship with God is restored. The burnt offering was wholly consumed and expressed full dedication. Thank offerings, todah, were shared meals of gratitude, and the willing, nadiv, gave freely.

Music was not decoration. The singers and players were organized by David at the LORD's command through Gad and Nathan, and the song began when the offering began. The chapter ends on joy and speed, and the note that the Levites were more diligent than the priests is a small, honest detail: the lesser order outdid the greater.
passages.later: Leviticus explains the blood: ‘For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you to make atonement for your souls upon the altar’ (Leviticus 17:11).
passages.hard:
Why did God require so much animal sacrifice, and what should a modern reader make of it?

The scale of the offerings can shock a modern reader. In the ancient world sacrifice was the ordinary language of worship in every culture, and Israel's system used that language to teach particular things: that sin is serious enough to cost a life, that God himself provides the means of cleansing, and that worship gives what is valuable. Much of the meat from peace and thank offerings was eaten by the worshipers, so these were also great shared feasts. The prophets insisted that sacrifice without obedience was worthless, and Jewish tradition after the temple's destruction in AD 70 turned to prayer, study and good deeds. Christians hold that the sacrifices were fulfilled and ended in Christ's death, as the letter to the Hebrews teaches. Readers of every view can agree that the chapter is not about God needing meat but about a people learning what it costs to be reconciled.
passages.asks: The Levites were more ready than the priests. Ask whether you have assumed that the people with titles will do what you could do yourself. And ask what willing gift you could bring that no one has asked of you.
